new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Spot-checks of the works marked silent in this folder's earlier check (all read from the saved text layers under: Dunn 1984 'The Papar language' (9,315-char text, pp.225-229): no occurrence of stress/accent/prominence/prosody/penult/syllable/phonology/pitch/tone, also with spaces stripped; it is location, population, lexicostatistics and intelligibility testing only. Miller 1984 'Introduction' (20,813 chars): no stress terms; the only 'phonological' is the survey-aims sentence 'known indigenous languages of Sabah including phonological, grammatical, and semantic studies', not a statement about any language. Lobel 2013 (888,920-char text): 13 lines contain 'stress'; none is within 3 lines of…

sources.citation: Gossens, A. L. 1924. A grammar and vocabulary of the Dusun language. Journal of the Malayan Branch of the Royal Asiatic Society 2(2): 87-220. (Glottolog Glottolog's most extensive description for papa1268, ref 42740)
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: a digital copy exists, behind a library sign-in
sources.note: Silent on word stress/accent. The 'Phonetics' section (pp.87-88, page scan read) covers vowel qualities, 'Each vowel is pronounced by itself', vowel length marked with macrons ('at least double the length of the ordinary a, i, o, u'), r/l/h interchange, and consonant doubling before -an/-on; three independent scanned copies of pp.87-220 a full-text search for stress/accent/stress/tonic: the only hit is 'if stress is desired' (p.89), meaning syntactic emphasis by adjective fronting. NB the sketch states (p.87) 'In this vocabulary I have followed the pronunciation of Kadazan as used in Papar' —…

sources.citation: Lobel, Jason William. 2013. Philippine and North Bornean languages: issues in description, subgrouping, and reconstruction. PhD dissertation, University of Hawai'i at Manoa. hdl:10125/101972
sources.note: Nothing on Papar stress. Ch.11 is a comparative phonology/subgrouping of Southwest Sabah languages; Papar [dpp] appears in cognate tables and in §11.4.1 'Tatana and Papar' (p.395), which locates the language in 'small patches of territory towards the northern tip of Kuala Penyu town' and reclassifies it as Greater Murutic; 'Dusun Papar'/'Kadazan Central Papar' are treated as separate Dusunic varieties. All 13 'stress' hits in the dissertation concern Philippine languages or a Blust quotation on schwa; none concern Papar.

sources.citation: Lobel, Jason William. 2013. Southwest Sabah revisited. Oceanic Linguistics 52(1): 36-68.
sources.note: The article that established Papar as a Greater Murutic language, based on phonological and morphological innovations; may contain phonological remarks (possibly on accent) on Papar not repeated in the dissertation. Paywalled (Unpaywall: not OA).

sources.citation: Dunn, Phyllis A. 1984. The Papar language. In Julie K. King & John Wayne King (eds), Languages of Sabah: a survey report, 225-229. Pacific Linguistics C-78. DOI 10.15144/PL-C78.225
sources.note: Nothing. Sociolinguistic survey chapter only: Papar spoken in two villages (Tinambak KP) in NW Kuala Penyu District, c. 600-800 speakers, ethnonym 'Bajau Bukit', legend of origin near Papar town but 'very low lexical relationship' with the language of Papar District; lexicostatistics and intelligibility tests. No phonology.

sources.citation: Miller, Carolyn P. 1984. Introduction. In King & King (eds), Languages of Sabah: a survey report. Pacific Linguistics C-78.
sources.note: Nothing (survey background and method; a full-text search for stress/accent/phonolog: no hits).

sources.citation: Smith, Kenneth D. 1984. The languages of Sabah: a tentative lexicostatistical classification. In Julie K. King & John Wayne King (eds), Languages of Sabah: a survey report, 1-49. Pacific Linguistics C-78.
sources.note: Wordlist-based classification that first listed Papar as a separate language; the SIL survey wordlists behind it are the only other primary Papar data. Unlikely to state a stress rule (lexicostatistics), so not downloaded; open at ANU.

sources.citation: Luering, H. L. E. 1897. A vocabulary of the Dusun language of Kimanis. Journal of the Straits Branch of the Royal Asiatic Society 30: 1-29. (archive.org biostor-176481)
sources.note: scanned text read only (not saved: it is Kadazan of Kimanis, a Dusunic variety, not Papar [dpp]). Its 'Pronunciation' note (pp.4-5) covers vowel and consonant values only; no stress statement.

sources.note: No phonology or stress information; confirm dpp = Greater Murutic per Lobel 2013/2016 and 'not to be confused with' Coastal Kadazan (coas1294, ISO kzj retired into dtp in 2015-060).

sources.note: The only modern first-hand data on Papar [dpp] (Lobel's own fieldwork; 594 lexical entries plus pronouns/demonstratives/case markers per language). If any published note on Papar phonology or stress exists, it is most likely in this book's introductory matter or in the transcription conventions of its Papar entries.

tone.summary: Comparative wordlist (500 items + 94 functors) with pronoun/demonstrative/case-marker tables for Papar; no phonology notes beyond an interdental lateral allophone of /l/; nothing on tone or stress.
